Figure 9: Air, glycol, and module temperatures during discharge at AHRI standard conditions Figure 10 shows the heat transfer and energy discharged from the system. During the majority of the discharging, the system delivered a cooling capacity of 3.5 RT and 4.51 RT-hr of total discharged energy until reaching the cutoff glycol temperature. The system COP during discharging is calculated as the ratio of heat transferred to the glycol stream and the electrical input to the system (glycol pump and fan power). The system COP was about 15. During discharging no latent cooling (moisture removal) was observed in the air stream. This is due to the relatively high inlet glycol temperature entering the cooling coil. This high temperature was a result of higher than anticipated thermal resistance between the glycol circuit and the thermal energy storage material. As shown in Figure 9 and Figure 11, the temperature of the glycol stream supplied by the modules remained close to 14°C which was unable to condense any moisture from the airstream. With improved thermal contact between the fluid tubes and the thermal energy storage, better heat transfer rates and energy utilization can be achieved from the system. 12 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications. Task 3: Gen-2 design Task Summary: Based on results from Task 2 experimental results, NREL will update the models for the PCM thermal storage module and HVAC system. The updated model, along with lessons learned from the first prototype build and characterization, will be used to update the new PCC design. In addition to the serpentine design, we also investigated the use of aluminum microchannels for the charge and discharge fluids. Multi-port extruded (MPE) aluminum channels are commonly used in air conditioning systems to reduce air-side pressure drop and increase heat transfer coefficients.
